Introduction and meaning
Force. BNS restatement of IPC 349. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 349. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 128 is the rule on “Force”. The section provides that a person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 128 exists so that “Force” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
128. A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:

(a) by his own bodily power;

(b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;

(c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move

Essential ingredients
1. A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:
2. (a) by his own bodily power;
3. (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;
4. (c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the following three ways, namely:–

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 128 (Force) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 128 (Force), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other’s body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other’s sense of feeling:
   (2) (a) by his own bodily power;
   (3) (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person;
   (4) (c) by inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 128 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 128 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

misconceptions.trap: Copying a statutory illustration without mapping it to an ingredient.
misconceptions.correction: Quote the illustration, then write which ingredient it proves or which ingredient is missing. Mapping is the core evidentiary link.
